title: Families reach last-minute agreement over disputed $180M Van Gogh sale | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

An agreement between the current ownersof a Vincent van Gogh painting and the heirs of a previous owner has been reached just a day before a blockbuster auction where the artwork isestimated to fetch$180 million. It follows claims that it was sold by a Jewish family “under duress” amid Nazi persecution in the 1930s.

The two families reached a “mutually satisfactory resolution” over the upcoming sale of “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”), Sotheby’s said in a statement, though the auction house did not elaborate on what the agreement involved.

The unnamed heirs of Samuel Fischer, a Jewish publisher living in Berlin before World War II, had initially objected to the Wednesday evening New York sale, arguing that their ancestors only sold the painting because of financial difficulties directly caused by the Nazi regime.

Their lawyer Gunnar Schnabel had written to Sotheby’s last Thursday, urging it to prove beyond doubt that the painting was sold at market value — and that the family would have done so “even without Nazi rule,” according to correspondence seen bythe New York Times. Schnabel, a Berlin-based lawyer specializing in Nazi-looted art, did not respond to CNN’s repeated requests for comment.

The day before the auction was set to go ahead, Sotheby’s declared “the matter resolved.” In its statement, the Fischer heirs said they were “grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration”with Sotheby’s and the current owners, the family of late Argentinian businessman Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his art patron wife, Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier. The Fischer heirs added that this made it “possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era.”

Likewise, the Blaquier-Arrietas said they were pleased to have reached an“amicable”resolution, adding: “We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”

Sotheby’s had earlier said its research had not established that the painting was sold under duress, but was committed to finding a resolution.

This dispute is the latest in a string of art market controversies surrounding paintings that, although not confiscated by Nazis, may have been sold under pressure or below market rate during the Third Reich era. Schnabel — who has not disclosed the US-based heirs’ identities — earliertold Sotheby’s that his clients were seeking a settlement “in the spirit of” the 1998 Washington Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art, a series of international guidelines on resolving disputes over holocaust-era assets, according to the New York Times.

Van Gogh painted “Châtaigniers en fleurs” in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise in 1890, shortly after his release from a psychiatric facility. In itscatalog, Sotheby’s said the vibrant street scene demonstrated “magnificent brushwork and an exuberant, expressive range of colors.”

Hungarian-born Fischer, founder of the publishing house S. Fischer Verlag, acquired it in Berlin in 1909. According to the Sotheby’s catalog, he deposited the painting with Paul Cassirer & Co., a gallery in Amsterdam, in either 1932 or 1933, the year the Nazi party came to power in Germany. Fischer died the next year, leaving his daughter and son-in-law, Brigitte and Gottfried Bermann-Fischer, in control of the family’s publishing house and his art collection.

In June 1936, Paul Cassirer & Co. sold the painting — which was still, at the time, in the Netherlands — to the French collectors Marcel and Henriette Kapferer on the Bermann-Fischers’ behalf. By this time, the pair had already fled Berlin for Vienna, where they established an Austrian branch of the family’s publishing house.

Schnabel reportedly believes this sale was necessitated by financial difficulties that the family business faced due to Nazi persecution. Some of the publisher’s high-profile authors, including Hermann Hesse and the Nobel Prize-winner Thomas Mann, had been blacklisted by the Nazi regime and their works ceremonially destroyed in book burnings.

While the Bermann-Fischers successfully smuggled some of the family’s art collection to Austria (before resettling in Sweden and eventually the US), Schnabel found that they were forced to pay the “Reich flight tax,” a substantial levy placed on the assets of people fleeing Nazi Germany, the Times reported.

Sotheby’s, meanwhile, believes there is no evidence that the sale was made under duress. The 1936 transaction was reportedly completed for 68,000 Swiss francs, then about $22,000. By comparison, Van Gogh’s painting “Verger avec cyprès,” which made history when it was sold for $117 million in 2022, sold for a reported $15,000 in 1935.

“Châtaigniers en fleurs” remains poised to break the auction record for Van Gogh’s work, set by “Verger avec cyprès.” The painting had been guaranteed by Sotheby’s, meaning that the seller has been promised a minimum price for the item, regardless of what happens at the sale. The auction house has not disclosed this floor price, though a spokesperson told CNN that if the painting “sells on the night, it will likely make a record for the artist.”

“Châtaigniers en fleurs” is one of 12 paintings — alongside works by Monet, Renoir and Cézanne — that Sotheby’s is offering from theBlaquier-Arrieta collection. It was purchased by the Argentinian family in 1975, having changed hands several times since World War II.

Because “Châtaigniers en fleurs” was sold in the Netherlands, which was not under Nazi occupation at the time, Fischer’s immediate heirs had little legal basis to seek compensation following World War II. But more recent — albeit non-binding — political agreements, including the 1998 Washington Principles and the 2009 Terezin Declaration (which explicitly references “forced sales and sales under duress”), have provided a new legal framework for descendants seeking restitution.

In 2022, France’s government returned a Gustav Klimt painting to the heirs of a Jewish family forced to sell it at a reduced price after the Nazis annexed Austria in 1938. The following year, heirs of Jewish collectors Karl Adler and Rosi Jacobifiled a lawsuitagainst New York’s Guggenheim Museum over a Pablo Picasso painting that they claimed had been sold in desperation while their ancestors fled persecution, though the case was dismissed in 2024.

Auction houses have typically avoided offering items that might fall foul of restitution claims, which can scare off potential buyers and attract criticism from Jewish advocacy groups. In 2023, amid growing public pressure, Sotheby’s rival Christie’scanceled asaleof around 300 pieces of jewelry from the collection of late art collector Heidi Horten, whose husband was accused of making his fortune by buying out Jewish businesses sold under duress in Nazi Germany.

With the Van Gogh dispute resolved, the 12 works from the Blaquier-Arrieta family’s collection remain poised to fetch a combined total of over $450 million. This represents a significant portion of the estimated $2 billion that will be spent at New York’s November auctions, which are held across the week at major auction houses including Sotheby’s, Christie’s, Phillips and Bonhams.

Early sales have already seen auction records set for modernist painter Wassily Kandinsky (whose “Betonte Ecken” sold for $85.8 million) and the late Japanese artistYayoi Kusama(whose “Way to Infinity: No. 3P.B.” fetched over $15 million).

Elsewhere, just hours before a planned auction, Christie’s postponed the sale of a Frida Kahlo painting that had previously been reported as missing from a Mexico City museum. In a statement, a spokesperson for the auction house said the artwork had been withdrawn “for further research,” adding: “We look forward to selling this work at a later date.”

This article was updated following the agreement between the Fischer heirs and the Blaquier-Arrieta family.

CNN’s Sheena McKenzie and Jacqui Palumbo contributed to this report.
